day-1.t: Day 1 — What a database actually is

b.v: Today's goal

v: Understand tables, rows and columns in plain words
Read the four-table shop database used in this course
Write and run your first SELECT

b.v: About 20 minutes. Use a free browser tool such as DB Browser for SQLite, or the SQL box in your course page.

A database is a set of tables. A table is like one sheet in Excel: columns are the fields, rows are the records. The difference is that a database can hold millions of rows and answer a question in a fraction of a second, without you dragging anything.
1) The vocabulary

v: Table = one list of one kind of thing, such as customers
Row = one record, such as one customer
Column = one field, such as a phone number
Primary key = the column that is unique for every row, such as customer_id
Foreign key = a column that points to another table, such as customer_id inside orders

b.v: Primary and foreign keys are how tables connect without repeating everything. The orders table stores customer_id 2, not the customer's name, city and phone. Change the phone number once and every order still points to the right person.
2) The shop database

v.cap: Table order_items: one row per product line. Order 1001 has two lines.

b.v: 3) Your first query

SELECT means show me. The asterisk means every column, and FROM names the table. End every statement with a semicolon. The second query below asks for fewer columns, which is faster and easier to check. SQL does not care about capital letters, but writing keywords in capitals makes a long query readable.
The most common beginner mistake is a missing semicolon or a misspelled table name. The error message is usually on the line you think is fine, so read it slowly instead of rewriting the query.
Practice

Create the four tables in a free SQLite tool and type the rows exactly as shown. Then write a query that returns only product name and price. You should see five rows, starting with Notebook at 150. Save the file as shop.db.
Today's goal

v: Filter rows with WHERE using numbers and text
Combine conditions with AND and OR
Sort results with ORDER BY, and limit the rows shown

b.v: About 20 minutes. Keep shop.db open from Day 1.
SELECT with no filter returns everything, which is rarely useful. WHERE is the part of SQL that turns a dump into an answer. It is also where beginners lose the most rows by accident.
1) Filter on a number
A number needs no quotes, as you can see in the query below. Run it and you get three products: Stapler at 700, Register at 400 and Pen pack at 250.

v: > = greater than
< = less than
>= = greater than or equal
<> = not equal, used instead of !=
BETWEEN 100 AND 200 = inside a range, including both ends

b.v: 2) Filter on text
Text values need single quotes. Only one customer lives in Lahore, Ayesha Khan, so you get one row back. Run it and count the rows yourself before trusting any query.
3) Two conditions and a sort
AND means both must be true. OR means either may be true. Use brackets when you mix them, because AND is read first and can quietly change your meaning.
ORDER BY sorts. ASC is smallest first and is the default. DESC is largest first. LIMIT 3 keeps the top three rows: Stapler 700, Register 400, Pen pack 250.

Text in SQL is case-sensitive in some databases and not in others, and a trailing space breaks an exact match. If a filter returns nothing, check the spelling and the spaces before you doubt the data.
Today's goal

v: Use COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX
Group rows by a column and total them
Filter groups with HAVING, not WHERE

b.v: About 20 minutes. This is the lesson that replaces most of your Excel pivots.
An aggregate takes many rows and returns one number. GROUP BY does it per category. Together they are the pivot table of the database world, and they work on a million rows without slowing down.
1) The five aggregates

v: COUNT(*) = how many rows
SUM(column) = the total of a number column
AVG(column) = the average, ignoring empty cells
MIN and MAX = the smallest and largest value
COUNT(DISTINCT column) = how many different values, ignoring repeats

b.v: Run it and you get 7 rows and 11,750 rupees. Check by hand: 1800 + 600 + 1200 + 800 + 2100 + 3000 + 2250 = 11,750. The AS word renames the output column, which makes the result readable.
2) Group by a column

Add GROUP BY and the same total is calculated for each group. Here is sales per product, using the order_items table joined to names by memory: product 1 is Notebook, 3 is Stapler, 4 is Marker, 5 is Register.

@SQL
SELECT product_id,
       SUM(quantity) AS units,
       SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS sales
FROM order_items
GROUP BY product_id
ORDER BY sales DESC;

Check the arithmetic: Notebook sells 12 + 8 + 20 + 15 = 55 units, and 55 times 150 is 8,250. Stapler is 3 units at 700, which is 2,100. Register 2 at 400 is 800. Marker 5 at 120 is 600. The four add to 11,750, the same grand total as before.

This returns customer 1 with 2 orders and customer 2 with 2 orders. Customer 3 has 1 order and customer 4 has none, so both are removed. Note that customer 4 does not appear at all — an aggregate cannot count rows that do not exist.
Every column in SELECT that is not inside an aggregate must appear in GROUP BY. Some databases allow the shortcut, others refuse. Write it correctly and your query works everywhere.
Practice

Write a query that shows, for each order_id, the number of lines and the order total. Then write one that returns only orders above 2,000 rupees using HAVING. Order 1001 is 2,400 and 1005 is 2,250, so you should get those two.
Today's goal

v: Join orders to customers to see names instead of numbers
Tell INNER JOIN from LEFT JOIN
Join three tables without duplicating the totals

b.v: About 20 minutes. Joins are the heart of SQL, so read this lesson twice if needed.

Real data lives in separate tables to avoid repetition. A JOIN sticks them back together for one query, matching rows on a shared column. Once you can join, you can answer almost any business question.
1) An inner join
INNER JOIN keeps only rows that match on both sides. Every order has a customer, so you see five rows with the name attached.

v: ON = the rule for matching rows, here customer_id equals customer_id
o and c = short aliases so you can say o.order_id instead of orders.order_id
Ambiguous column = a name that exists in both tables and must be prefixed with its alias

b.v: 2) A left join keeps the misses
LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the first table, even when there is no match. Unmatched columns come back empty, shown as NULL. This is how you find customers who never ordered.

v.cap: The four customers with their order counts

b.v: Sana Malik appears with 0. With an INNER JOIN she would vanish, and you would wrongly believe every customer is buying. COUNT(o.order_id) counts only real matches; COUNT(*) would count her one unmatched row and wrongly show 1.
3) Three tables, and the duplicate trap

@SQL
-- six lines, because 1005 is pending and filtered out
-- totals: 2400 + 2000 + 2100 + 3000 = 9500
SELECT o.order_id, p.name AS product, i.quantity, i.quantity * i.unit_price AS line_total
FROM orders AS o
INNER JOIN order_items AS i ON o.order_id = i.order_id
INNER JOIN products AS p ON i.product_id = p.product_id
WHERE o.status = 'paid';
If a total doubles or triples after adding a join, you have created duplicate rows. Group by the right key, or use DISTINCT. Never fix a duplicated total by dividing by two.
Practice
Write one query that lists every order with the customer name and city. Then write a LEFT JOIN query that finds customers with zero orders. Sana Malik must appear, or your join direction is wrong.
Today's goal

v: Use a subquery inside WHERE to compare against a computed value
Use IN to filter against a list produced by another query
Save a query as a view so nobody has to retype it

b.v: About 20 minutes. Read from the inside out, like brackets in maths.
Sometimes the filter you need is itself a query. 'Show products priced above average' has no fixed number in it. A subquery answers the inner question first, then the outer query uses the answer.
1) A subquery that returns one value
The inner query gives 324, because 150 + 250 + 700 + 120 + 400 is 1,620 and 1,620 divided by 5 is 324. The outer query then keeps the products above 324: Stapler at 700 and Register at 400.
2) IN with a list from another query
Here the inner query finds who bought at least twice, then the outer query returns their details. This is often clearer than a join with HAVING, because the two steps are separate.
The result is Ayesha Khan in Lahore and Bilal Ahmed in Karachi. Customer 3 has one order and customer 4 has none, so neither is in the inner list.
3) Save it as a view

A view is a saved query with a name. It stores no data, so it never goes out of date. Views are the easiest way to give a colleague a safe, simple table without giving them the base tables. A correlated subquery, by contrast, is an inner query that refers to the outer row: powerful, but slower.

@SQL
CREATE VIEW paid_order_totals AS
SELECT o.order_id, c.name, SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS total
FROM orders AS o
JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'paid'
GROUP BY o.order_id, c.name;
After that you can simply write SELECT * FROM paid_order_totals ORDER BY total DESC. The first row is order 1004 for Farhan Ali at 3,000.
A subquery inside IN must return exactly one column. Two columns is an error, and beginners often add the name 'to make it clearer'. Keep only the key.
Practice

Write a query that lists products priced above the average price. You should get exactly two rows. Then create the view paid_order_totals and run it with ORDER BY total DESC to confirm 3,000 is at the top.
Today's goal

v: Write an UPDATE that touches exactly the rows you intend
Use a transaction so a mistake can be undone
Add a new row with INSERT without breaking keys

b.v: About 20 minutes. Work on a copy of shop.db, named shop-test.db.

Reading data is safe. Writing data is not. One missing word in an UPDATE can change every row in the table, and there is no undo button in most databases. Today you learn the habits that make writing safe.
1) Test with SELECT first
Before any UPDATE, run the same WHERE in a SELECT and count the rows. If the SELECT shows one row, the UPDATE will change one row.

v: UPDATE table SET column = value WHERE ... = change rows that match
Always include WHERE, even when you think you want all rows
Run the WHERE as a SELECT first, every single time

b.v: 2) Use a transaction

A transaction groups statements so that either all of them happen or none do. You write BEGIN, do the work, check the result, then COMMIT. If anything looks wrong, ROLLBACK and the table is exactly as before.
Stapler stock was 12. Selling 3 leaves 9. If the check had shown 0 or a negative number, the next line would be ROLLBACK instead of COMMIT, and the stock would go back to 12.
3) Insert a row
INSERT adds rows. If a column is missing from your list, it gets NULL or a default. If you insert a duplicate primary key, the database refuses, which is a feature, not a bug.
UPDATE products SET price = 200; with no WHERE changes every product in the shop. This is the mistake that ends in a restored backup and a bad evening.
Practice

On your copy of the database, change the stock of product 4 from 60 to 55 to record a sale of 5 markers. Use BEGIN, the UPDATE, a SELECT check and COMMIT. Then add customer Hina Riaz and confirm she appears in a SELECT.

day-7.t: Day 7 — Indexes, speed and the cost of a bad query

b.v: Today's goal

v: Understand what an index does, in plain words
Know which columns deserve one
Recognise the query habits that make a database slow

b.v: About 20 minutes. No numbers to memorise — just a clear picture.

An index is like the index at the back of a textbook. Without it, the database reads every page to find one name. With it, the database jumps straight to the right page. Nothing about your data changes; only the speed of finding it.
1) What an index costs

v: Faster reads = finding rows by that column becomes quick
Slower writes = every insert and update must also update the index
Extra space = the index is stored beside the table
Best for columns used in WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY

b.v: Primary keys are indexed automatically, which is why joins on customer_id are fast. A foreign key used in every join is the next best candidate for an index you add yourself.
2) Habits that ruin speed
Small changes in how you write a query can turn a fast lookup into a full scan of every row. These four appear in real workplace code all the time.

v: Wrapping a column in a function, as in WHERE YEAR(order_date) = 2026, which stops the index being used
SELECT * when you need two columns, which moves data you never read
LIKE '%khan' with a leading percent sign, which cannot use an index
No LIMIT while exploring, which pulls a million rows to your phone

b.v: 3) How to check

Every database has a way to show the plan: EXPLAIN in SQLite and PostgreSQL, EXPLAIN in MySQL too. It tells you whether the database used an index or scanned the whole table, without running the query for real.

Check a slow query:|Put EXPLAIN in front of the SELECT|Look for the words scan or search on the big table|If it says scan and the table is large, add an index on the filter column|Run EXPLAIN again and compare
Do not index every column 'just in case'. Twenty indexes make inserts slow and confuse the planner. Index the columns you actually filter and join on.
Practice

Run EXPLAIN on a query filtering orders by customer_id before and after creating idx_orders_customer. On a five-row table the difference is invisible — write one sentence explaining why the index still matters at 500,000 rows.

day-8.t: Day 8 — The mistakes that delete data

b.v: Today's goal

v: Know the four statements that destroy data and how they differ
Build a habit list that prevents 95 percent of accidents
Practise recovery thinking before you need it

b.v: About 20 minutes. Read this one even if you never plan to write to a database.

Most data loss is not a hacker. It is a tired person at 9 pm running a statement on the production database that they meant to run on a test copy. The statement takes a tenth of a second and the recovery takes a weekend.
1) The four dangerous statements

v: DELETE FROM orders = removes every row, table still exists
UPDATE without WHERE = rewrites every row
DROP TABLE orders = removes the table and the data
TRUNCATE TABLE orders = empties it fast, and often cannot be rolled back

b.v: DELETE with a WHERE is normal work. DELETE without one is a disaster. The difference is nine characters, which is why the habit of writing the WHERE first matters so much.
2) The habit list

Before every write:|Confirm which database you are connected to, by name|Run the WHERE as a SELECT and read the rows|Wrap the change in BEGIN and COMMIT|Keep a recent backup you have actually restored once|Never run a write on production from your phone
That last one is not a joke. A phone screen hides the connection name, and a small keyboard makes typos likely. Real shops have lost their sales tables this way.
3) Recovery thinking
Ask two questions today, before anything goes wrong. How often is the database backed up, and who has restored one to prove it works? A backup nobody has tested is a hope, not a backup.

v.cap: A five-line safety sheet to keep beside your desk
rows: Test and live look identical in a query window
Shows the exact rows before you change them

b.v: Never test a DELETE on the live database because it is 'just one row'. Copy the database, or use a transaction. One row is how the first accident starts.
Practice

On your test copy, run BEGIN, then DELETE FROM orders with no WHERE, then SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders to see zero rows, then ROLLBACK and count again. Seeing the rows come back teaches the value of a transaction better than any warning.

day-9.t: Day 9 — Answer five real business questions

b.v: Today's goal

v: Turn five plain English questions into working queries
Check every answer against the tables by hand
Keep the queries in a file so you can reuse them

b.v: About 25 minutes. This is the lesson where SQL becomes useful at work.
A manager does not ask for a JOIN. They ask who is buying, what sells, and who owes money. Your job is the translation, and then a number you can defend when someone questions it.
1) Who are my best customers?

Sales per customer, largest first. Ayesha bought 2,400 and 2,100, so 4,500. Bilal bought 2,000 and 2,250, so 4,250. Farhan bought 3,000. Sana bought nothing and does not appear, because an inner join needs a match.

@SQL
SELECT c.name, SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS sales
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY c.name
ORDER BY sales DESC;
2) Which products sell in units but not in rupees?
This is the question that changes buying decisions. Notebook sells 55 units for 8,250 — the best on both measures. Marker sells 5 units for only 600, so it takes shelf space without paying rent.

@SQL
SELECT p.name,
       SUM(i.quantity) AS units,
       SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS sales
FROM order_items AS i
JOIN products AS p ON p.product_id = i.product_id
GROUP BY p.name
ORDER BY units DESC;
3) Who has not paid, and which city is growing?
Two short queries. The first finds pending orders with a name attached. The second totals sales by city; note that Islamabad has no sales and therefore no row, which is itself useful information.

@SQL
SELECT o.order_id, c.name, o.order_date
FROM orders AS o
JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'pending';

SELECT c.city, SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS sales
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY c.city
ORDER BY sales DESC;

Pending: order 1005 for Bilal Ahmed. By city: Lahore 4,500, Karachi 4,250, Multan 3,000, adding to 11,750. Every query in this lesson gives the same grand total, which is how you know the joins are sound.
If two different queries give two different grand totals, stop and fix it. Do not choose the number you prefer. A dashboard built on a wrong join is worse than no dashboard.
Practice

Write all five queries into a file called shop-queries.sql with a comment above each one stating the question in English. Add a sixth of your own: average order value per city, and check that the three city averages sit between 2,000 and 3,000.

day-10.t: Day 10 — Your SQL toolkit and next steps

b.v: Today's goal

v: Revise the eight clauses that cover most real queries
Know what to learn next and in what order
Build a personal cheat sheet you will actually use

b.v: About 20 minutes. Finish with one clean cheat sheet, not ten bookmarks.
You now know enough SQL to be useful at work. Most reporting questions in a small business need only SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, JOIN and ORDER BY. The rest is practice and a little patience.
1) The order clauses run in
SQL is written in one order and read in another. Knowing the reading order explains most confusing errors, especially why WHERE cannot see a SUM.

v.cap: Write this on a card and stick it near your screen

b.v: 2) A cheat sheet worth keeping
3) What to learn next

v: Practice on one real dataset you care about, for a month
Learn CASE WHEN, which puts if-then logic inside a query
Learn window functions, which rank rows without collapsing them
Learn how your workplace backs up and restores its database

b.v: Do not collect ten SQL courses and finish none. One dataset, fifty queries, and a habit of checking totals will teach you more than any certificate.
Practice

Write your own one-page cheat sheet by hand, using your own words, with the seven clauses in reading order and three queries from this course. Keep shop-queries.sql beside it. Then teach the GROUP BY lesson to one colleague in ten minutes — teaching is the fastest way to find the gap in your own understanding.
